title: Ledger Equalities
statement: An auditor writes facts about single-letter accounts as strings like "a==b" (the two accounts hold the same amount) or "a!=c" (they hold different amounts). Given the list of equations, return true if some assignment of amounts makes every fact true at once, and false otherwise.
constraints: Each equation has the form x==y or x!=y with lowercase letters x and y

examples.explanation: a and b cannot be both equal and different.
All three hold when a, b and c share an amount.

hints.content: Equalities chain together: if a==b and b==c, then a==c.
Group letters that must be equal; an inequality is violated exactly when both its letters land in the same group.
Process all equalities first, then check the inequalities.
A disjoint-set (union-find) structure over 26 letters tracks the groups.
Union the letters of every '==' equation, then for each '!=' check that the two letters have different roots.

testCases.explanation: a and b cannot be both equal and different.
All three hold when a, b and c share an amount.
Order does not matter: still a contradiction.

solutions.title: Transitive closure table
solutions.intuition: Compute which letters must be equal by closing the equality relation, then test the inequalities.
solutions.approach: Start a 26 × 26 table with each letter equal to itself and every '==' pair. Apply Floyd–Warshall-style closure (if i~k and k~j then i~j). Then every '!=' pair must be unrelated.
solutions.pseudocode:
same[i][i] = true; mark == pairs both ways
for k, i, j: if same[i][k] and same[k][j]: same[i][j] = true
return all != pairs have same == false
commonMistakes: Checking inequalities before all equalities are applied.
Forgetting that a letter equals itself.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The transitive closure makes the equality groups explicit. With only 26 letters the cubic closure is cheap, but it doesn't scale to large variable sets.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: a==b, b==c mark a~b and b~c; closure adds a~c.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: c!=a finds same[c][a] true: return false.

solutions.title: Union equalities, then check inequalities
solutions.intuition: Equality is an equivalence relation, so union-find computes its classes directly.
solutions.approach: Union the two letters of every '==' equation. Then return false if any '!=' equation has both letters with the same root.
commonMistakes: Interleaving unions and checks in input order, which misses equalities that appear later.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Equalities define equivalence classes, so I union all '==' pairs first and then check every '!=' pair for a shared root. Order matters only in that two-phase sense. It runs in near-linear time, and the same idea extends to arbitrary variable names with a map from names to indices.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Union a,b and b,c: all share one root.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: c!=a: same root, so return false.
